claims_disputed.claim: Formal traceability is traded for input flexibility: only controlled-input or model-based approaches produce requirements-to-test traceability, and fully generative LLM studies produce none
claims_disputed.reason: Table IV codes every LLM study's K4 as 'Low - none reported', so the deficit measures what papers report, not what pipelines can do. None of the nine LLM studies set out to emit a traceability matrix. The 'trade-off' (§VI-D gap finding 1) is a pattern across 8 hand-coded studies with no second coder, not a measured trade within any study. The narrow observation (no LLM study in this corpus reports a traceability artifact) holds, but the causal 'traded for' does not.

claims_disputed.claim: Test-generation accuracy degrades with requirement complexity
claims_disputed.reason: Only one cited study actually stratifies by requirement complexity: Medeshetty et al. (§V-C Table I, 95/75/60%). That is a rule-based extractor, not LLM test generation, and per-category sample sizes are not given. Korraprolu's 'MCDC <= 50.2% vs ~79% decision coverage' compares two coverage criteria on the same 25 requirements, so it measures criterion strictness, not degradation as requirements get more complex. The GPT-4 vs Mistral-7B gap is a model contrast on identical inputs.

pattern_stance_changes.reason: 'Mixed' requires a split isolating comparison. The survey runs none, and the primary results it cites (SPECMATE 56%, CiRA 71.8%, boilerplate 10% on Npac) are not contrasts of structured vs unstructured requirements on the same task. It reports P34-adjacent results secondhand, so 'neutral'.

missed_issues: Ten of 26 primary studies (38%) came from outside the core database query: five by backward snowballing on Yang et al.'s reference list (§III-D, folded into the '21') and five from a later supplementary search. The PRISMA arithmetic also leaves 16 studies after eligibility (136 full texts, 120 excluded), not 21. The exact-phrase AND query therefore had poor recall, which undermines the 'first focused synthesis' and corpus-wide claims more than the review states.

Per-study quality scores (QA1-QA4) are never shown, so the claim that 'all twenty-six met the minimum threshold of 2.0' (§III-E) cannot be checked. The acknowledgments credit a non-author with 'supporting data analysis', and no inter-rater agreement is reported for screening, quality scoring or Table IV coding.

Inclusion criterion I4 excludes code-to-test and agentic test generation, so nothing in the corpus concerns coding agents writing tests in a repository. Transfer to an agent harness for a Java team is limited to the requirement-form point.

LLM4Fin's ChatGPT baseline is given as 'approximately 19 minutes' (§V-B, Fig. 5) and '20 minutes' (Table II) per generation against 6.99 seconds. The survey repeats this implausible latency contrast without asking what it measures.
note: My blind scores match the review's exactly, and I agree with the verdict and with its grading of the gap matrix, the hallucination argument and the novelty claim as weak. I go further on the two claims the review left at moderate. The traceability 'trade-off' rests on coding 'none reported' as Low across eight hand-picked studies. The complexity-degradation claim has only one stratified primary study, and that is rule-based, while the MCDC evidence measures coverage-criterion strictness. I also move P34 from mixed to neutral because the survey makes no isolating comparison. The search-recall problem (38% of studies found outside the query) is larger than the review indicates.
